title: Esther 4:1–11
context: When Mordecai learns of the decree, he tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and wails loudly in the city, coming as far as the king’s gate, which no one may enter in sackcloth (4:1–2). Throughout the provinces the Jews mourn with fasting, weeping, and wailing (4:3). Esther, grieved, sends clothing that Mordecai refuses, and she sends the eunuch Hathach to learn what has happened (4:4–6). Mordecai tells Hathach everything, including the exact sum Haman promised, gives him a copy of the decree, and charges Esther to go to the king and plead for her people (4:7–8). Esther replies that anyone who approaches the king in the inner court uncalled faces death unless the king holds out the golden scepter, and that she has not been called for thirty days (4:9–11). The scene shows the Jews’ grief and Esther’s hidden identity (2:10, 2:20) colliding with the danger of the court. The book does not mention prayer in these verses, and it does not name God; many readers in both traditions assume that sackcloth and fasting carry an implicit appeal to God, but this commentary notes that as an inference. On how prayer and fasting relate to God’s purposes, compare the discussion at Joshua 10:14.

verses.text: Now when Mordecai found out all that was done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and wails aloud in the city. Arminian readers see public lament as a fitting and honest response to evil, and they note that Mordecai feels the weight of the decree personally, since his refusal to bow was the spark Haman used. Grief here is not passivity but the beginning of action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read sackcloth and ashes as traditional signs of mourning and humbling before God (compare Joel 2:12–13 and Jonah 3:6), though the book does not name God or record a prayer. Shared ground: both traditions read the lament as genuine and fitting, and both are careful to describe any implied appeal to God as an inference from these customary signs rather than a stated fact.

verses.text: He came even before the king’s gate, for no one is allowed inside the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai comes as far as the king’s gate but cannot enter in sackcloth. Arminian readers note that the court shields the king from the grief his decree has caused, a quiet critique of power insulated from the suffering it inflicts. Mordecai’s presence at the gate makes the grief visible to those who would rather ignore it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the barrier at the gate as the narrator’s comment on a court that keeps sorrow out of sight, and they read Mordecai’s position as a step toward bringing the crisis before the throne through Esther. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a social detail with moral weight and avoid making it carry more than the narrator says about Persian custom.

verses.text: In every province, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
verses.arminianNotes: Wherever the decree arrives, the Jews mourn with fasting, weeping, wailing, sackcloth, and ashes. Arminian readers see a whole community responding to danger with lament, and many assume, without the text saying so, that such fasting implied turning to God. They stress that real human responses matter in the unfolding of God’s faithful care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that fasting in Scripture is often joined to seeking God (compare Joel 2:12), and they read the community’s mourning as the humbling that often precedes deliverance in the biblical pattern. Shared ground: both traditions note that the book does not mention prayer here, treat any implied prayer as an inference, and point to the discussion at Joshua 10:14 for questions about how prayer relates to God’s purposes.

verses.text: Esther’s maidens and her eunuchs came and told her this, and the queen was exceedingly grieved. She sent clothing to Mordecai, to replace his sackcloth, but he didn’t receive it.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther hears, is deeply grieved, and sends clothing so Mordecai can remove his sackcloth, but he refuses it. Arminian readers see Esther’s first response as genuine care, perhaps also a wish to quiet the public display, and Mordecai’s refusal as a deliberate signal that the crisis cannot be solved by covering it. Esther is moved toward a choice she has not yet made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read Esther’s gift as loving but insufficient, and Mordecai’s refusal as a way of pressing the true situation on her. They see God drawing Esther step by step into the role she will play, through ordinary human interactions. Shared ground: both traditions note that the text does not state Esther’s full motive and read the exchange as preparing for Mordecai’s charge in 4:8.

verses.text: Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs, whom he had appointed to attend her, and commanded him to go to Mordecai, to find out what this was, and why it was.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther calls Hathach, a eunuch appointed to attend her, and sends him to find out what is happening and why. Arminian readers see Esther moving from distance to inquiry, a small but real step in which she chooses to engage rather than look away. Her seclusion in the palace shows how isolated she has been from events outside.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the queen does not know what has happened, which underscores how secret her identity has remained (2:10, 2:20), and they see the go-between as part of the ordinary means through which the story moves forward. Shared ground: both traditions read Hathach’s errand as the opening of a dialogue that will test Esther, and neither claims more than the text reports.

verses.text: So Hathach went out to Mordecai, to the city square which was before the king’s gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Hathach goes out to Mordecai in the city square before the king’s gate. Arminian readers note the careful staging, with Mordecai outside and Esther inside, separated by custom and walls, so that every word must pass through a messenger. The distance makes Esther’s eventual decision more clearly her own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the separation and see the narrator slowing the action so that readers feel the weight of the crisis. The faithful service of a minor figure like Hathach is part of how events are carried forward. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as a narrative bridge and avoid assigning it a theological meaning beyond the setting it provides.

verses.text: Mordecai told him of all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai tells Hathach everything that happened to him, including the exact sum Haman promised the treasuries for the Jews’ destruction. Arminian readers see Mordecai giving Esther full information so that she can make a responsible decision, and they note that he does not hide his own part in the crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Mordecai’s thoroughness and read the mention of the exact sum as showing that this was a purchased destruction, deliberate and calculated (compare 3:9). They see truthfulness as the ground of wise action. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Mordecai laying out the facts plainly, and both note that he knows details of the bargain that the narrator does not explain how he learned.

verses.text: He also gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given out in Susa to destroy them, to show it to Esther, and to declare it to her, and to urge her to go in to the king to make supplication to him, and to make request before him for her people.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai sends a copy of the decree and urges Esther to go to the king and plead for her people. Arminian readers note that Mordecai appeals to Esther’s will and conscience, asking her to reveal the identity she had hidden (2:10, 2:20). The call presents a real choice with real risk, and Esther is free to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the charge as a summons to Esther to identify with her people, and they see God working through Mordecai’s urging as an ordinary means of providence. Shared ground: both traditions note the phrase “for her people,” which marks the turning point of Esther’s hidden identity, and both read the charge as weighty without assuming the outcome is in doubt from God’s side.

verses.text: Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
verses.arminianNotes: Hathach returns and tells Esther Mordecai’s words. Arminian readers note that the messenger faithfully relays the words without softening them, so that Esther now faces the full weight of the request. Her response will be her own, made with full knowledge of the danger to her people and to herself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hathach’s faithful report as a small act of integrity on which much depends. They note that the narrator keeps the focus on Esther’s decision, the hinge of the story. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a transition, and both see faithfulness in small duties as part of how deliverance comes, without forcing any theological dispute onto it.

verses.text: Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and gave him a message to Mordecai:
verses.arminianNotes: Esther gives Hathach a reply for Mordecai. Arminian readers note that Esther does not simply comply but answers with her own concerns, a sign that her decision will be considered and real. The book presents her as a thoughtful agent rather than a passive tool of others’ plans.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe that Esther’s first reply raises an objection, which mirrors other biblical callings where a hesitant servant voices fear before acting (compare Exodus 3:11 and 4:10). Shared ground: both traditions take Esther’s hesitation seriously and sympathetically, and both see the dialogue as the means by which she comes to resolve.

verses.text: “All the king’s servants and the people of the king’s provinces know that whoever, whether man or woman, comes to the king into the inner court without being called, there is one law for him, that he be put to death, except those to whom the king might hold out the golden scepter, that he may live. I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther explains that anyone approaching the king in the inner court uncalled faces death unless he holds out the golden scepter, and that she has not been summoned for thirty days. Arminian readers stress that her fear is reasonable, given what happened to Vashti (1:19), and that the danger makes her eventual decision a genuine act of courage rather than a foregone outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the real danger and note the uncertainty of Esther’s standing after thirty days without a summons. They see the obstacle as one that only an unexpected turn can overcome, which the story will narrate (5:2). Shared ground: both traditions read Esther’s caution as honest and not cowardly, and both avoid speculating about Persian court law beyond what the text reports.
